meta.title: Who really said "I've failed over and over and over again in my life, and that is why I succeed"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Michael Jordan really said it, in Nike's 1997 “Failure” ad. But the words were scripted by copywriter Jamie Barrett, not composed by Jordan.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I've failed over and over and over again in my life, and that is why I succeed'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine: Michael Jordan spoke this line in Nike's 1997 “Failure” commercial. The twist — the copy was written for him by ad man Jamie Barrett.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Jordan really said this — word for word — in Nike’s 1997 television commercial “Failure.” The line is documented in Wikiquote’s sourced section, citing Nike Culture: The Sign of the Swoosh (1998), p. 49. One catch: the words were scripted for him by ad copywriter Jamie Barrett, not composed by Jordan himself.

source.heading: The Nike “Failure” commercial, 1997

docMeta.dd: Nike Culture: The Sign of the Swoosh (1998), p. 49

source.excerpt: I’ve missed more than 9,000 shots in my career. I’ve lost almost 300 games. 26 times I’ve been trusted to take the game-winning shot and missed. I’ve failed over and over and over again in my life. And that is why I succeed.
trail: Wikiquote lists the full voiceover in its sourced section, citing Nike Culture: The Sign of the Swoosh (1998), p. 49.
Encyclopedia.com’s Nike entry credits “Wieden & Kennedy’s Jamie Barrett” with writing the script for the “9,000 Shots” spot from his own knowledge of Jordan’s career.
Sneaker Freaker reproduces the line and dates the “Failure” ad to 1997.
source.excerptNote: The famous line is the last two sentences; it is almost always quoted apart from the “9,000 shots” opening that sets it up.
source.rightsHolder: Nike, Inc. (advertising copy by Jamie Barrett / Wieden+Kennedy)
source.rightsNote: The line is scripted advertising copy first published in a 1997 Nike television commercial and reproduced in a 1998 book — well after 1931, so it is in copyright in the United States. Rights rest with Nike, Inc.; the words were written by copywriter Jamie Barrett of Wieden+Kennedy.

author.name: Michael Jordan
author.heading: About Michael Jordan
author.metaLine: b. 1963 · Hall-of-Fame basketball player · Chicago Bulls
author.bio: Michael Jordan (b. 1963) is a six-time NBA champion with the Chicago Bulls and among the most decorated players in basketball history. By the late 1990s he was also one of the world’s most bankable pitchmen, and Nike’s “Failure” spot fused his on-court legend with a message about persistence. The voiceover—delivered in his voice, about his own career—was written for him by Wieden+Kennedy copywriter Jamie Barrett.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Michael Jordan is correct — he really speaks this line. The subtler misconception is authorship: the words are usually presented as Jordan’s own spontaneous wisdom, when they were a professionally written ad script.

items.scope: the words as his own composition
items.why: Jordan spoke the line, but he did not write it. Encyclopedia.com’s Nike entry credits Wieden+Kennedy copywriter Jamie Barrett with writing the “9,000 Shots” script.
The quote is routinely trimmed or reworded — the “9,000 shots” and “26 times” setup is dropped and the numbers drift — even though the closing sentences are reproduced accurately by Wikiquote.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Michael Jordan’s spoken line from Nike’s 1997 “Failure” commercial — but the words were scripted by copywriter Jamie Barrett, per Encyclopedia.com.

context.heading: Why the line stuck
lead: Nike’s “Failure” aired in 1997, at the height of Jordan’s fame. Rather than sell shoes with highlights, it counted his failures — missed shots, lost games, blown game-winners — and reframed them as the engine of his success.

The gambit worked partly because the arithmetic was real: copywriter Jamie Barrett estimated Jordan’s missed shots from memory and simple math, and his guess held up when he later checked the numbers.
context.pull: “I’ve failed over and over and over again in my life. And that is why I succeed.”
